`CLAUDE.md`:

```md
# CLAUDE.md: working on iG Windows Tuner

## Hard rule for development sessions

**The development machine is the user's real gaming PC.** Run only read-only operations on it:

- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Report`, `-ListTweaks`, `-DryRun`, `Get-IgwtTweakState`, `Get-IgwtPlan`, health and detection functions, and `Show-IgwtGui -RenderTo <folder>` (offscreen screenshots).
- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Clean -Scan` / `Invoke-IgwtCleanerScan` (enumerates and sizes, deletes nothing) and `-Analyze <path>` / `Get-IgwtDiskUsage`.
- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Hardware [-Json]` / `Get-IgwtHardwareProfile` and `Resolve-IgwtPresetSelection` (read-only).
- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Asr` (without change options), `-Asr ... -DryRun`, `-AsrAudit`, `-SecurityScore`, `-NetworkSurface` / `Get-IgwtAsrStatus`, `Get-IgwtAsrAudit`, `Get-IgwtSecurityScore`, `Get-IgwtNetworkSurface`, `Get-IgwtLocalAccountAudit` (read-only; the Defender log is read with `Get-WinEvent`).
- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Inspect <areas>`, `-PowerSetting ... -DryRun` / `Get-IgwtInspection`, `Get-IgwtPowerSettingChangePlan` (read-only; `powercfg /qh` is a read).
- `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Inventory <view>`, `-Change ... -DryRun`, `-Persistence [-ReportPath]`, `-Updates`, `-Diagnostics <areas>`, `-SystemReport -ReportPath` / `Get-IgwtServiceInventory`, `Get-IgwtTaskInventory`, `Get-IgwtAppInventory`, `Get-IgwtPersistenceInventory`, `Get-IgwtUpdateStatus`, `Get-IgwtFirewallRuleList`, `Get-IgwtHostsFile`, `Get-IgwtAdapterPropertyInspection`, `Get-IgwtDiagnostics`, `Get-IgwtManagedChangePlan`, `Get-IgwtSystemReport` (read-only). `-DnsBenchmark` and `-Latency` send network traffic and change nothing; run them only when the user asks.
- The Pester suite (non-elevated; it uses `TestRegistry:` and mocks only), PSScriptAnalyzer, and `tools\Test-Catalog.ps1` / `tools\Build-Docs.ps1`.
- A Defender custom scan of the project folder (`tools\Invoke-QualityChecks.ps1`).

**Never** run `-Apply`, `-Preset` without `-DryRun`, `-Revert`, `-RevertAll`, `-ResetDefault`, `-Clean` without `-Scan`, `-Asr` with `-AsrMode`/`-AsrRecommended`/`-AsrExclude`/`-AsrUnexclude` without `-DryRun`, `-PowerSetting` without `-DryRun`, `-Change` without `-DryRun`, `Invoke-IgwtManagedChange`, `Invoke-IgwtApply`, `Invoke-IgwtRevert`, `Invoke-IgwtCleanerClean`, `Invoke-IgwtAsrChange`, `Invoke-IgwtPowerSettingChange`, `Set-IgwtStartupItemEnabled`, or anything that changes the registry, services, power plans, adapters, firewall or Defender on this machine. End-to-end apply/revert testing happens only in Windows Sandbox (`tools\iGWindowsTuner.wsb`), and the user runs it.

## Architecture in one paragraph

`data\tweaks\*.json` (schema v2, `docs\SCHEMA.md`) declares every tweak (id, texts, `level`, evidence, impact, risk, `antiCheat`, `reversible`, `sideEffects`, `requires`, `appliesTo`, `hardware`, `source`, typed `actions`). The loaders also accept v1 entries and upgrade them in memory (`src\Core\Migration.ps1`); `tools\Convert-IgwtV1Data.ps1` rewrites v1 files. The computed properties `expert`, `antiCheatSafe` and `tier` exist only in memory. The engine (`src\Core\Engine.ps1`) dispatches each action type through explicit `switch` statements to `src\Actions\<Type>.ps1`. Each action type implements: **State** (detect), **Snapshot** (capture exact previous data), **Apply** (`on` or Windows `default`) and **Restore** (from snapshot). `src\Core\StateDetection.ps1` rolls item states up to On / Off / Partial / NotApplicable / ManagedByPolicy / Unknown. The CLI (`iGWindowsTuner.ps1`) and the GUI (`src\Gui`) only call engine functions; the GUI worker runspace calls exported commands with `AddCommand`.

## How to add a tweak

1. Verify the setting against current Microsoft or vendor documentation for build 26100+ (path, value, type, Windows default). Popularity is not evidence. Record deviations in `docs\DECISIONS.md`.
2. Add an entry to the right `data\tweaks\<category>.json`:
   - `id` as `category.name` in lower case; `hint` of 140 characters or less; a 2-4 sentence `description` (what, why, trade-off, how to revert).
   - `evidence.tier` `A` (documented) or `B` (situational: the hint or description must say "measure"), with at least one https source.
   - Schema v2 fields: `level` (Standard, Advanced, Expert, Lab), `antiCheat` (`"safe"`, `"unknown"` or `{ "breaks": [...] }`), `reversible` (full, partial, none), `sideEffects` (text, required unless fully reversible), `source` (igwt, winutil + `attribution`, microsoft), `hardware` (`tags`/`excludeTags` from `data\hardware\tags.json`), and `appliesTo` (`minBuild`, optional `maxBuild`, `editions`, `conditions`). Write the file with `ConvertTo-IgwtJson` style (2-space indent, ASCII) or run `tools\Convert-IgwtV1Data.ps1`, which also normalizes formatting.
   - Registry actions need `valueType`, `on` and `default` (`"<absent>"` when the value does not exist by default). Use `absentValue` when Windows treats a missing value as a specific value, `equivalentOn` for other values that count as on, `bitClear` to clear flag bits, and `onlyIfAbsent` for create-only values.
   - Prefer existing action types (1.0 types plus 2.0: storageSense, wufbPolicy, deviceInterrupt, serviceSet, powercfgAttribute, powercfgSettingAcDc, scheduledTask, firewallRule, appx, winget, capability, processMitigation, exploitSystem, cleanerRule; `check` with checker DefaultApp). A new type needs State/Snapshot/Apply/Restore, entries in the four dispatch switches (`StateDetection.ps1`, `Engine.ps1`), identifying fields in `Get-IgwtActionFingerprint`, rules in `Test-IgwtV2Action`, a description in `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` and a round trip in `tests\Handlers.Tests.ps1`. For a one-off handler, add Detect/Snapshot/Apply/Restore to `$script:IgwtCustomHandlers` in `src\Actions\Custom.ps1`.
   - An item that breaks anti-cheat is level `Lab` with `antiCheat: { "breaks": [...] }`; unknown impact needs Expert or Lab. Expert and Lab items need a `warning`. Never change an existing action's identifying fields (type, path, name, item, ...): snapshots match actions by fingerprint.
3. Add the id to a preset's `include` only when it fits the preset rules (level at or below `levelCeiling`, never Lab; gaming presets only `antiCheat: "safe"`; Balanced = Tier A only; no conflicting pairs).
4. Run `tools\Test-Catalog.ps1`, then the Pester suite, then `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` (regenerates `docs\TWEAKS.md`, `docs\PRESETS.md`, `docs\REJECTED_TWEAKS.md` and `docs\CLEANER.md`).
5. Rejected ideas go to `data\rejected.json` with a reason, never into the catalog.
6. Renaming an id: add `"old": "new"` to `data\migration\id-map.json` so old snapshots and presets still resolve.

## How to add a hardware tag or overlay

1. New tag: add it to `data\hardware\tags.json` (id, name, group, hint, description) and a detection rule to `data\hardware\detection.json` (`when` keys are ANDed, `anyOf` is OR; keys: cpuVendor, cpuName, cpuNameNot, cpuFamily, cpuModels, hybrid, gpuName, gpuPnp, nicName, nicPnp, laptop, vm, modernStandby, systemDiskBus, systemDiskMedia, memoryGBMin, memoryGBBelow). Never use HypervisorPresent for VM detection.
2. New overlay: add it to `data\hardware\overlays.json` with `id` `overlay.*`, `tags` (any of), `hint`, `description`, `basis` (vendor, reviewer, igwt), https `sources`, and at least one of `block` (item ids), `blockMatching` (action fields such as type/setting/handler/name, or `fieldPresent`), `add` (item ids) and `guidance`.
3. Add or update a fixture in `tests\fixtures\hardware` (capture real facts with `.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Hardware -Json`; no serial numbers) and assert the tags and preset effects in `tests\Hardware.Tests.ps1`. Then run `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` (regenerates `docs\HARDWARE.md`).

## How to add or change an ASR rule

1. Check the rule against the Microsoft Learn ASR reference and overview (GUID, Warn support, cloud dependency, server-only, standard vs other).
2. Edit `data\asr\rules.json`: `id` (GUID), `key` (lower-case-hyphenated), `name`, `category` (standard, other), `msCategory`, `order`, `hint` (140 characters or fewer), `description`, `gamerImpact` and `gamerImpactLevel` (none, low, medium, high), `supportsWarn`, `requiresCloud`, `appliesTo` (office, adobe, exchange or empty), `serverOnly`, `recommendedMode` (standard rules Block; medium/high gamer impact never Block; server-only NotConfigured), `notes`, https `sources`. Never change a GUID: ASR snapshots refer to it.
3. Run the Pester suite (`Test-IgwtAsrCatalog` runs inside `Test-IgwtCatalog`) and `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` (regenerates `docs\ASR_CENTER.md`).
4. ASR changes go through `Invoke-IgwtAsrChange` only (snapshot operation `ASR`, revert through `Invoke-IgwtRevert`). Exclusions are ASR-only and must pass `Test-IgwtAsrExclusion`; antivirus exclusions are never added.

## How to extend the expert inspectors

- **Power plan editor:** add a processor setting to `data\power\processor.json` (`alias`, `guid`, `group`, `level` Advanced/Expert, `hint` of 140 characters or fewer, `description`, https `sources`). Ranges come from `powercfg /qh` at runtime; hardware overlays (`data\hardware\overlays.json`, `blockMatching` with `type: powercfgSetting`) decide where it is blocked. Processor idle disable must never be added.
- **Kernel and memory inspector:** add keys or values to `data\inspectors\kernel.json` (`name`, `default` or `<absent>`, optional `absentMeans`, `meaning`, optional `item` (catalog id) or `rejected` (rejected id), `sources`). The inspector stays read-only: a value becomes changeable only through a catalog item.
- Run the Pester suite (`Test-IgwtPowerSettingCatalog` and `Test-IgwtKernelInspectorCatalog` run inside `Test-IgwtCatalog`) and `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` (regenerates `docs\INSPECTORS.md`).

## How to extend the management modules

- **Protected services:** add names or wildcard patterns with a reason to `data\manage\services.json`; `Test-IgwtManageCatalog` (inside `Test-IgwtCatalog`) also requires the spec section 12 core list. Protected tasks come from `$script:IgwtProtectedTaskPaths` (`src\Actions\ScheduledTask.ps1`) plus the anti-cheat pattern in `src\Manage\ManagedChange.ps1`; protected apps from `Test-IgwtAppxProtected`; protected features and capabilities from `src\Manage\ManagedChange.ps1`.
- **New change kind:** extend `New-IgwtManagedAction` so it validates the target and returns an action of an existing, tested type; never add a write path outside `Invoke-IgwtManagedChange` (snapshot operation `Manage`, revert rebuilds and re-validates the action).
- **Curated sets** (such as telemetry tasks) are catalog items, not hard-coded lists in the module.
- **NIC keyword descriptions:** `data\manage\nic-keywords.json` (standardized `*` keywords only, with the Microsoft source).
- Everything else in `src\Manage` (inventories, persistence, update status, network toolkit, diagnostics, system report) stays read-only; tests mock every system call (`tests\Manage.Tests.ps1`).

## How to add a cleaner rule

1. Find the vendor's documented cache location (or mark the rule Tier B). Never point a rule at user documents, profile roots or program folders: the denylist in `src\Cleaner\CleanerSafety.ps1` refuses them anyway.
2. Add it to `data\cleaner\<category>.json` with `id` `clean.*`, `level`, `tier`, `method`, `hint`, `description`, `sideEffects`, `antiCheat: "safe"`, `reversible` (none, or partial for Recycle Bin rules), `source`, `hardware`, and `roots` (or `userDataRoots` + cache folder names for browsers). List apps that must be closed in `requiresClosed`; only Standard rules may be `default: true`.
3. Run the Pester suite (`tests\Cleaner.Tests.ps1` validates the catalog) and `tools\Build-Docs.ps1`.

## Tests

```powershell
# non-elevated Windows PowerShell
Import-Module Pester -RequiredVersion 5.7.1
Invoke-Pester -Path .\tests -Output Detailed
Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path . -Recurse        # uses PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1 (documented exclusions)
.\tools\Invoke-QualityChecks.ps1              # all of the above plus the Defender scan
```

- Tests call `Initialize-IgwtTestEnvironment` (`tests\TestHelpers.ps1`), which redirects `HKLM:\` and `HKCU:\` into `TestRegistry:` and turns on TestMode. In TestMode, any registry path that escapes the redirect throws, and `powercfg`/`nvidia-smi` throw unless mocked.
- Mock system cmdlets with `Mock <Cmdlet> -ModuleName iGWindowsTuner`. Note that many NetAdapter/NetQos/DnsClient parameters are `string[]`, so index `[0]` in mocks.
- The suite refuses to run elevated (`IGWT_ALLOW_ELEVATED_TESTS=1` only inside Windows Sandbox).

## Conventions

- PowerShell 5.1 syntax: no ternary, `??`, `?.` or `-AsHashtable`. Keep source files ASCII.
- `[Math]::Min`/`Max` with an integer literal and a double picks the integer overload and truncates (`[Math]::Max(0, 0.5)` is 0): cast both arguments to `[double]`. `@($genericList)` throws in Windows PowerShell 5.1: use `.ToArray()`. A single `[pscustomobject]` has no `.Count` in 5.1: wrap results in `@()`.
- Inside double-quoted strings, write `${var}?` (PowerShell would otherwise parse `$var?` as a variable named `var?`). Avoid nested double quotes with backtick escapes inside `$()`.
- Functions use the `Igwt` noun prefix; state-changing ones support `-WhatIf`. Keep comment-based help on every function.
- Never add `Invoke-Expression`, Base64, downloads, hidden windows, persistence, `bcdedit`, Defender antivirus exclusions or AMSI/ETW changes (ASR-only exclusions exist only in the ASR Center). `tests\Safety.Tests.ps1` will fail.
- Every function name must be unique across `src\` (a later file silently replaces an earlier definition); `tests\Safety.Tests.ps1` checks it. Reuse existing helpers such as `Test-IgwtPathUnder -Path -Parent`.
- No tweak logic in the GUI.

```

# iG Windows Tuner 2.0: progress tracker

This file lets any session resume exactly where the last one stopped. Update it after every phase.

- **Target version:** 2.0.0
- **Working rule:** development on the real target PC is read-only. Allowed: `-Report`, `-DryRun`, `-Clean -Scan`, detection and inspectors, `winget list` / `winget search`, Pester (TestRegistry, temp fixtures, mocks), PSScriptAnalyzer, and a Defender custom scan of the project folder.

## Baseline (16 Oct 2026)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Pester 5.7.1 (`tests\`) | 132 passed, 0 failed |
| PSScriptAnalyzer (`-Recurse`, project settings) | 0 findings |
| Defender custom scan (v1 release) | no threats |

No baseline failures to record.

### Version control

- **git is not installed** on this PC (`git` is not on PATH), and installing it would violate the read-only development rule (no installs). So there is no repository, tag or `v2` branch yet.
- Substitute for the `v1-baseline` tag: the full v1 tree is archived at `C:\IntelGates Tune\AegisTune-v1-baseline.zip`
  (SHA256 `CEF6AE17559ADFC422A48228688585B316C61947232CEFC322459C8765F1816E`).
- Phase checkpoints are recorded below (date + tests) instead of commits. Once git is installed, run:

```bash
git init && git add -A && git commit -m "chore: import iG Windows Tuner" && git tag v1-baseline
```

  Do this on a checkout of the baseline zip, then commit the v2 tree on a `v2` branch.

### Spec files

- `SPEC.md` (v1) was not present in the repository. The v1 requirements are captured in `CLAUDE.md` and `docs\` (README, SECURITY, ANTICHEAT, DECISIONS, TESTING). The v2 specification is the one provided in the session; deviations are recorded in `docs\DECISIONS.md` as they are made.

## Scope notes (decided up front; details in docs\DECISIONS.md as phases land)

- The v1 invariants stay: no BCD writes, no test signing or kernel debugging, no disabling of Defender, firewall, UAC, DEP, SmartScreen, Windows Update or speculative-execution mitigations.
- Items that would turn off platform security features or break kernel anti-cheat are not added as new toggles. The existing warned VBS/HVCI expert toggle from v1 is kept unchanged.
- "Expert" items are limited to documented, reversible tuning: power-plan attributes and processor settings, device interrupt mode and affinity policy, NIC queues, crash-dump and page-file configuration. All of them come with read-only inspectors first.

`PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1`:

```psd1
# PSScriptAnalyzer settings for iG Windows Tuner (picked up automatically when analyzing this folder).
# Every exclusion is a deliberate, documented decision (see docs/TESTING.md):
@{
    Severity     = @('Error', 'Warning', 'Information')
    ExcludeRules = @(
        # Every action type implements the same signature (Action, Context, Mode, Snapshot) so the
        # engine can dispatch uniformly; implementations that do not need a parameter still accept it.
        'PSReviewUnusedParameter',
        # A handful of internal functions intentionally return collections and are named for it
        # (Get-IgwtPowerSchemes, Get-IgwtInstalledGames, Get-IgwtRejectedTweaks, ...).
        'PSUseSingularNouns',
        # Informational: functions return PSCustomObjects/hashtables shaped by the JSON catalog.
        'PSUseOutputTypeCorrectly'
    )
}

`README.md`:

```md
# iG Windows Tuner

**An auditable, reversible Windows 11 tuner for competitive gaming that keeps your PC secure and your anti-cheat happy.**

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows%2011%20Pro-0078D4)
![PowerShell](https://img.shields.io/badge/PowerShell-5.1%20%7C%207.4-5391FE)
![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pester-506%20passing-2EA44F)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-lightgrey)
![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-preview-orange)

## Why this exists

Most "gaming optimizer" scripts make the same trade: paste a few hundred registry edits from a forum, disable Defender, Windows Update and virtualization-based security, and hope the frame rate goes up. The result is often placebo, sometimes slower, frequently less secure, and increasingly incompatible with kernel anti-cheat (Riot Vanguard, FACEIT, Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, RICOCHET, Javelin), which now *requires* TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, VBS and HVCI.

iG Windows Tuner takes the opposite approach:

- **Evidence first.** Every change is documented by Microsoft or the hardware vendor (Tier A), or is real but situational and clearly marked "measure before and after" (Tier B). Popular tweaks that are placebo, obsolete or harmful are not hidden. They are listed with the reason they were rejected.
- **Everything is reversible.** Before anything changes, the exact previous value (including its type, or the fact that it did not exist) is written to a JSON snapshot, and a System Restore point is created. Any change can be reverted individually or all at once.
- **Security goes up, not down.** Defender, the firewall, UAC, SmartScreen, Windows Update, VBS/HVCI and Secure Boot are never weakened. The tool includes hardening such as attack surface reduction rules, LSA protection and encrypted DNS.
- **Anti-cheat compatible by design.** Nothing that anti-cheat depends on is touched, and readiness for each major anti-cheat is checked and shown.
- **Transparent.** Every registry path, service, power setting and policy is shown as "current -> target" before you apply anything. Nothing is downloaded, obfuscated or hidden.

## What it does

| Area | Highlights |
|---|---|
| **Presets** | Competitive, Balanced and Hardened, adjusted automatically to your hardware (hybrid Intel CPUs, AMD X3D, laptops, VMs and more). |
| **Tweak catalog** | 84 verified items across Power & CPU, Graphics & Display, Input, Network, Background & Privacy, Security, Storage and System, each with a hint, a description, sources and a revert path. |
| **Health report** | Read-only checks of firmware, microcode, Secure Boot, VBS/HVCI, GPU (Resizable BAR, refresh rate), network adapter, storage and an anti-cheat readiness score. HTML export. |
| **ASR Center** | All 19 Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction rules with modes, gamer-impact notes, per-rule exclusions and an audit view of what each rule blocked. |
| **Security score** | 25 weighted checks, each with the exact fix, plus a local accounts audit and a listening-ports report. |
| **Expert inspectors** | Power plan (hidden processor settings included), interrupts and MSI mode, network queues, kernel and memory values, timer, crash dumps, all next to their Windows defaults. |
| **Cleaner** | Allow-list rules for temp files, caches and logs with a scan that deletes nothing, plus a disk analyzer and Storage Sense policies. |
| **Manage** | Services with a safe-to-change rating, scheduled tasks, apps, an Autoruns-style persistence inspector with signature checks, and a firewall rule browser. |
| **Diagnostics** | DPC/ISR time, reliability history, crashes and minidumps, boot performance, driver inventory, Windows Update status, DNS benchmark, latency and jitter test, and a full system report. |

The WPF interface follows the Windows 11 design language and starts **read-only**. It asks for administrator rights through the normal UAC prompt only when you choose to apply something.

## Quick start

Requirements: Windows 11 Pro 24H2 or newer (build 26100+), and Windows PowerShell 5.1, which is built in. PowerShell 7.4 also works. No installation and no dependencies.

1. Download or clone this repository.
2. Double-click **`Start-iGWindowsTuner.cmd`** to open the GUI. It starts in read-only mode.

Or use the command line (read-only commands need no elevation):

```powershell
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Report                      # health and anti-cheat readiness
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -ListTweaks                  # every item with its tier, risk and current state
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Preset Competitive -DryRun  # exactly what a preset would change; changes nothing
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -SecurityScore               # security score with the fix for each finding
```

Changes are applied and undone like this (each one writes a snapshot first):

```powershell
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Preset Balanced
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -Revert input.pointer-precision-off
.\iGWindowsTuner.ps1 -RevertAll                   # undo the most recent apply
```

If you downloaded a zip, Windows marks the files as coming from the internet. Review them, check them against `SHA256SUMS.txt`, and then unblock them (`Get-ChildItem -Recurse | Unblock-File`).

## What it never does

- Edit BCD, enable test signing, disable driver signature enforcement, or turn off DEP, ASLR or CFG.
- Touch Secure Boot, TPM, firmware, voltages, power limits or anti-cheat services, or install drivers.
- Disable Defender, Tamper Protection, AMSI, ETW, the firewall, UAC, SmartScreen or Windows Update, or add antivirus exclusions.
- Create persistence (scheduled tasks, services, Run keys, WMI subscriptions), hide windows, download anything, or change your execution policy.

These rules are enforced by a static safety test suite that runs against the source code.

## How it is built

- **Data-driven.** The catalog lives in `data\*.json` (schema v2). The engine dispatches typed actions (registry, service, power plan, firewall, QoS, scheduled task, and more), and each action type implements detect, snapshot, apply and restore.
- **Plain PowerShell.** It is readable, modular and has comment-based help on every function. It uses one documented P/Invoke (`SystemParametersInfo`) and no compiled binaries.
- **Tested.** 506 Pester tests run against Pester's `TestRegistry:` drive and mocks only, so the suite never touches the real system. PSScriptAnalyzer reports zero findings, and a Microsoft Defender scan runs as part of the quality checks (`tools\Invoke-QualityChecks.ps1`).
- **Safe end-to-end testing.** `tools\iGWindowsTuner.wsb` runs apply and revert inside Windows Sandbox.

## Project status

This is a **preview** of version 2.0. The engine, catalog, hardware profiles, cleaner, ASR Center, security modules, expert inspectors and management/diagnostic modules are complete and covered by tests. Still planned: a curated toolkit section, custom presets with drift detection, a GUI command palette and timeline, and the full end-to-end Sandbox verification before a stable release. The roadmap is tracked in [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md).

Run the read-only commands and `-DryRun` first, and review what a change does before you apply it.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome, provided they follow the evidence rule: a new item needs a current Microsoft or vendor source (or a Tier B "measure" label), a hint, a description, a revert path and tests. Start with [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md), which is the contributor guide, then run `tools\Invoke-QualityChecks.ps1` before opening a pull request.

`Start-iGWindowsTuner.cmd`:

```cmd
@echo off
rem iG Windows Tuner launcher.
rem Starts the GUI with the inbox Windows PowerShell 5.1 in a visible window (STA for WPF).
rem "-ExecutionPolicy Bypass" applies to this PowerShell process only; the machine and user
rem execution policies are never changed. iG Windows Tuner starts read-only; it asks for elevation
rem through the normal UAC prompt only when you choose to apply changes.
rem Pass parameters through, for example:  Start-iGWindowsTuner.cmd -Report
setlocal
set "IGWT_SCRIPT=%~dp0iGWindowsTuner.ps1"
"%SystemRoot%\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe" -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -STA -File "%IGWT_SCRIPT%" %*
set "IGWT_EXIT=%ERRORLEVEL%"
endlocal & exit /b %IGWT_EXIT%
```

`data/schema/cleaner-rule.schema.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "$id": "https://igwindowstuner.local/schema/cleaner-rule.schema.json",
  "title": "iG Windows Tuner cleaner rule file (schema v2)",
  "type": "object",
  "required": [ "schemaVersion", "rules" ],
  "properties": {
    "schemaVersion": { "const": 2 },
    "category": { "type": "string" },
    "rules": { "type": "array", "items": { "$ref": "#/definitions/rule" } }
  },
  "definitions": {
    "rule": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": [ "id", "name", "category", "level", "tier", "method", "hint", "description", "sideEffects", "antiCheat", "reversible", "source", "hardware" ],
      "properties": {
        "id": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^clean\\.[a-z0-9\\.\\-]+$" },
        "name": { "type": "string" },
        "category": { "enum": [ "System", "Gaming", "Browsers", "Apps", "Developer", "Downloads" ] },
        "level": { "enum": [ "Standard", "Advanced", "Expert" ] },
        "tier": { "enum": [ "A", "B" ], "description": "A: the location or method is documented by Microsoft or the vendor (see sources). B: a well-known cache location without a vendor document." },
        "method": { "enum": [ "files", "browserCache", "recycleBin", "deliveryOptimization", "dism", "driverStore", "guidance" ] },
        "default": { "type": "boolean", "description": "Selected by default (Standard rules only)." },
        "hint": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "maxLength": 140 },
        "description": { "type": "string", "minLength": 40 },
        "sideEffects": { "type": "string" },
        "antiCheat": { "const": "safe" },
        "reversible": { "enum": [ "full", "partial", "none" ], "description": "none: deleted permanently; partial: Recycle Bin; full: nothing is changed (guidance)." },
        "source": { "enum": [ "igwt", "winutil", "microsoft" ] },
        "attribution": { "type": "string" },
        "hardware": { "type": "object", "properties": { "tags": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } }, "excludeTags": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } } } },

`docs/ANTICHEAT.md`:

```md
# Anti-cheat compatibility

iG Windows Tuner must never break kernel-level anti-cheat. This page records the current platform requirements (verified during development on 16 Oct 2026), how iG Windows Tuner detects them, and the rules that follow from them.

## Requirements by anti-cheat

| Anti-cheat | TPM 2.0 | Secure Boot | VBS | HVCI | IOMMU / DMA protection | Windows | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FACEIT AC** (CS2) | Required | Required | Required (waves) | - | Required (waves) | Windows 11 from 14 Oct 2026 | TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot have been mandatory for all players since 25 Nov 2025. IOMMU and VBS were rolled out in waves (limited rollout from April 2025; required above 3,000 Elo from August 2025). FACEIT says VBS is required for IOMMU to work reliably. |
| **Riot Vanguard** (VALORANT, LoL), classic | Required on Windows 11 | Required on Windows 11 | - | - | - | - | Vanguard's own error codes (VAN 9001/9003) enforce TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot on Windows 11. |
| **Riot Vanguard On-Demand mode** (optional) | Required | Required | Required | Required | Required | Windows 11 **25H2+** | Uses the Runtime Driver Attestation Report that ships with 25H2. VGTray's Pre-Check lists anything still missing. |
| **Call of Duty** (RICOCHET) | Required | Required | - | - | - | - | Mandatory since Black Ops 7. |
| **Battlefield 6** (Javelin) | Required | Required | - | - | - | - | Kernel-level anti-cheat. |
| **Easy Anti-Cheat / BattlEye** | - | Per game | - | - | - | - | No platform-wide requirement. Test signing and kernel debugging are refused. |
| **VAC** (Dota 2, CS2) | - | - | - | - | - | - | User-mode anti-cheat with no platform requirement. |

Sources:

- FACEIT: <https://support.faceit.com/hc/en-us/articles/23117181142556> (Windows security requirements FAQ), <https://support.faceit.com/hc/en-us/articles/22851956652956-Known-issues-with-Anti-Cheat-Requirements>. Both blocked automated download (HTTP 403), so their content was verified through search results and news coverage. The Windows 10 cut-off date (14 Oct 2026) comes from secondary coverage, for example <https://www.dust2.us/news/66964/faceit-announces-major-anti-cheat-update>.
- Riot Vanguard On-Demand: <https://support.riotgames.com/en-us/riot/support-tools/vanguard-pre-check> (fetched; lists Windows 11 25H2 or newer, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, IOMMU, VBS, HVCI), plus <https://www.tomshardware.com/video-games/pc-gaming/riot-vanguard-adds-an-on-demand-mode-that-stops-anti-cheat-loading-at-boot-on-secured-windows-11-pcs>.
- Call of Duty and Battlefield 6: <https://www.guru3d.com/story/call-of-duty-black-ops-7-system-requirements-tpm-20-and-secure-boot>, <https://www.thesixthaxis.com/?p=462600>.
- VBS, HVCI and DMA properties: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/enable-virtualization-based-protection-of-code-integrity>.

## How iG Windows Tuner detects readiness (read-only)

| Requirement | Detection |
|---|---|
| TPM 2.0 ready | Elevated: `Get-Tpm` (present/ready) plus the `Win32_Tpm` spec version. Not elevated: the "Trusted Platform Module 2.0" PnP device and its status (labelled "presence only"). |
| Secure Boot on | `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecureBoot\State\UEFISecureBootEnabled`; `Confirm-SecureBootUEFI` when elevated. |
| Secure Boot 2023 certificates | `...\SecureBoot\Servicing\UEFICA2023Status` (`Updated`), `WindowsUEFICA2023Capable` (2 = booting the 2023-signed boot manager), `UEFICA2023Error`. Elevated runs also check that `db` contains "Windows UEFI CA 2023" and `KEK` contains "KEK 2K CA 2023". Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011 expires on **19 Oct 2026**, and the report flags this prominently. iG Windows Tuner never triggers certificate deployment (`AvailableUpdates`); it points to Windows Security > Device security > Secure Boot. |
| VBS running | `Win32_DeviceGuard.VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus = 2` |
| HVCI running | `Win32_DeviceGuard.SecurityServicesRunning` contains 2 |
| IOMMU / Kernel DMA protection | `Win32_DeviceGuard.AvailableSecurityProperties` contains 3 ("DMA protection is available"). msinfo32's "Kernel DMA Protection" line gives a second confirmation. |
| Windows 11 / 25H2+ | Build >= 22000 / >= 26200 |
| No test signing / kernel debugging | `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SystemStartOptions` (read only; BCD is never read or written) |

The **Dashboard** shows each requirement plus a per-anti-cheat pass/fail matrix. The header pill is:

- **Green**: everything passes, including Vanguard On-Demand prerequisites and the 2023 certificates.
- **Amber**: the kernel anti-cheats work, but an optional mode or the 2023 certificates are missing.
- **Red**: a hard requirement fails (TPM, Secure Boot, or test signing active).

On the target PC (i7-13700K, Z690 AORUS MASTER, 26H2 build 26300.9711) the read-only report shows **Green**: TPM 2.0 present, Secure Boot on, 2023 certificates applied (`Updated`, capable = 2), VBS and HVCI running, DMA protection available.

## Rules enforced in code

- The classic "disable VBS / Memory Integrity for FPS" tweak is **excluded from every preset** (enforced by `Test-IgwtCatalog` and the Pester suite). It exists only as the expert toggle `sec.vbs-hvci-off-expert`. That toggle needs `-AcknowledgeRisk` on the CLI or a confirmation dialog in the GUI, and shows a red warning that names FACEIT and Vanguard.
- Every catalog entry declares `antiCheatSafe`. A tweak that is not anti-cheat safe must be an expert toggle with a warning, and may not appear in a preset.
- Services `vgc`, `vgk`, `FACEIT*`, `EasyAntiCheat*`, `BEService`, `BEDaisy` and the core security services are on a hard deny-list in the service action, so the engine throws even if a catalog entry tried to change them.
- No BCD access, test signing, driver signature changes, kernel debugging, DEP/ASLR/CFG changes, Secure Boot or TPM changes, driver installs, or game process/file access. Static tests in `tests\Safety.Tests.ps1` scan the shipped source for these.
- `sec.hvci-on` (Tier A, in every preset) keeps memory integrity on; its "reset to Windows default" is also on.
- Kernel-mode hardware-enforced stack protection (`sec.kernel-shadow-stacks`) is a manual Tier B toggle, because some older anti-cheat drivers were incompatible with it.

```

`docs/ASR_CENTER.md`:

```md
# ASR Center and security score

> Generated by `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` from `data\asr\rules.json` and `src\Security\SecurityScore.ps1`. Do not edit by hand.

Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction (ASR) rules block behaviors malware relies on. The ASR Center (GUI page, `-Asr`, `-AsrAudit`) shows every rule with its mode, what it means for games, launchers and mods, and the exclusions that apply to it. Modes iG Windows Tuner can set: Not configured (Windows default), Audit, Warn (where supported) and Block. It never writes an explicit Off and never changes server-only rules or rules managed by Group Policy or MDM. Every change writes a snapshot first and can be reverted from Backups & Logs or with `-RevertAll -Snapshot <file>`.

Recommended modes for a gaming PC: the three standard protection rules and the rules without gamer impact in Block; rules that can catch games, launchers or mods in Audit, so you can review the audit view first. `-AsrRecommended` only ever raises a rule.

| Rule | Key | Category | Gamer impact | Recommended | Warn | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers | `vulnerable-drivers` | Standard protection | low | Block | yes |  |
| Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem | `lsass` | Standard protection | none | Block | no |  |
| Block persistence through WMI event subscription | `wmi-persistence` | Standard protection | none | Block | yes |  |
| Block executable content from email client and webmail | `email-executable` | Email | none | Block | yes |  |
| Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content | `script-downloads` | Script | none | Block | yes |  |
| Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts | `obfuscated-scripts` | Script | low | Block | yes | needs cloud protection |
| Block untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB | `usb-untrusted` | Polymorphic threats | low | Block | yes |  |
| Block rebooting machine in Safe Mode | `safe-mode-reboot` | Misc | none | Audit | yes |  |
| Block use of copied or impersonated system tools | `copied-system-tools` | Misc | medium | Audit | yes |  |
| Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion | `prevalence-age` | Polymorphic threats | high | Audit | yes | needs cloud protection |
| Use advanced protection against ransomware | `ransomware` | Polymorphic threats | medium | Audit | yes | needs cloud protection |
| Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands | `psexec-wmi` | Lateral movement & credential theft | medium | Audit | yes |  |
| Block all Office applications from creating child processes | `office-child-processes` | Productivity apps | none | Audit | yes | Office |
| Block Office applications from creating executable content | `office-executable-content` | Productivity apps | none | Audit | yes | Office |
| Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes | `office-injection` | Productivity apps | none | Audit | no | Office |
| Block Office communication application from creating child processes | `outlook-child-processes` | Email, Productivity apps | none | Audit | yes | Office |
| Block Win32 API calls from Office macros | `office-macro-win32` | Productivity apps | none | Audit | yes | Office |
| Block Adobe Reader from creating child processes | `adobe-child-processes` | Productivity apps | none | Audit | yes | Adobe Reader |
| Block Webshell creation for Servers | `webshell-servers` | Misc | none | NotConfigured | yes | Exchange servers only |

## Rules

### Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers

`56a863a9-875e-4185-98a7-b882c64b5ce5` | key `vulnerable-drivers`

Prevents applications from writing vulnerable signed drivers (drivers with known flaws that malware and some cheats load to get kernel access) to disk. Drivers that are already installed are not affected; the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist covers loading. Microsoft lists it as a standard protection rule that can go straight to Block.

- **Gamer impact (low):** None for games or anti-cheat. Old RGB, fan-control or overclocking tools that ship a known-vulnerable driver may fail to install it.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-abuse-of-exploited-vulnerable-signed-drivers>

### Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem

`9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2` | key `lsass`

Blocks processes from opening the Local Security Authority (LSASS) process with memory-read access, the technique credential dumpers use. When LSA protection is on, the rule adds no extra protection but does no harm. Expect block events for svchost.exe, updaters and monitoring tools: they are only denied access to LSASS memory, not stopped from running. Warn mode is not supported.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None. Block events for Windows services and launcher updaters are expected noise that Microsoft says can be ignored; nothing stops working.
- **Notes:** Redundant when LSA protection (sec.lsa-protection) is on. Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem>

### Block persistence through WMI event subscription

`e6db77e5-3df2-4cf1-b95a-636979351e5b` | key `wmi-persistence`

Blocks the creation of permanent WMI event subscriptions, a fileless persistence technique where malware keeps its trigger in the WMI repository instead of on disk. Microsoft lists it as a standard protection rule; the only known conflict is the Configuration Manager client, which home PCs do not use.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Only tools that create permanent WMI event subscriptions are affected, which consumer software rarely does.
- **Notes:** Test in Audit first on PCs managed by Configuration Manager. Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-persistence-through-wmi-event-subscription>

### Block executable content from email client and webmail

`be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550` | key `email-executable`

Stops executable files (exe, dll, scr), scripts (ps1, vbs, js) and archives opened from Outlook, Outlook.com and other popular webmail services from running. Malicious attachments are still one of the most common ways malware arrives. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline (sec.asr-baseline) already sets it to Block.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Executable attachments opened from mail are blocked; save them through a browser download if you trust the sender.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail>

### Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content

`d3e037e1-3eb8-44c8-a917-57927947596d` | key `script-downloads`

Malware written in JavaScript or VBScript often only downloads and starts the real payload. This rule blocks scripts from launching executables they fetched from the internet. A few old installers use such a script stub, but games and launchers do not. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Old installers that use a VBScript or JScript stub to download and start an exe may fail.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content>

### Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts

`5beb7efe-fd9a-4556-801d-275e5ffc04cc` | key `obfuscated-scripts`

Detects suspicious properties of obfuscated scripts, which malware uses to hide what it does. It covers PowerShell and relies on AMSI and cloud-delivered protection, so it only works fully with cloud protection on. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.

- **Gamer impact (low):** Low. A few mod installers or tweak scripts that pack their code can be blocked; games and launchers themselves are not affected.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts>

### Block untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB

`b2b3f03d-6a65-4f7b-a9c7-1c7ef74a9ba4` | key `usb-untrusted`

Prevents unsigned or untrusted executable files from running from removable drives, including SD cards. Copying files from the drive still works; files copied to the disk are judged where they run. iG Windows Tuner's gaming-safe baseline already sets it to Block.

- **Gamer impact (low):** Low. Unsigned portable tools started straight from a USB stick are blocked; signed programs and copying files are not affected.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-untrusted-and-unsigned-processes-that-run-from-usb>

### Block rebooting machine in Safe Mode

`33ddedf1-c6e0-47cb-833e-de6133960387` | key `safe-mode-reboot`

Ransomware sometimes restarts Windows in Safe Mode, where many security products do not run, before encrypting files. This rule blocks commonly abused commands such as bcdedit and bootcfg from setting a Safe Mode boot. You can still reach Safe Mode through the Windows Recovery Environment (Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced startup).

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Troubleshooting guides that set Safe Mode with bcdedit will not work; use Advanced startup instead.
- **Notes:** Microsoft lists it under the rules to test in Audit first.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-rebooting-machine-in-safe-mode>

### Block use of copied or impersonated system tools

`c0033c00-d16d-4114-a5a0-dc9b3a7d2ceb` | key `copied-system-tools`

Treats the programs in System32 and SysWOW64 as Windows system tools and blocks copies or same-named files that run from other locations, even when signed. Microsoft notes that its heuristics can also flag legitimate third-party programs that run from non-default install paths. Audit first and add a per-rule exclusion for any trusted program it reports.

- **Gamer impact (medium):** Medium. Games, launchers or tools installed in custom folders can match the heuristics; check the audit view before switching to Block.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-use-of-copied-or-impersonated-system-tools>

### Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

`01443614-cd74-433a-b99e-2ecdc07bfc25` | key `prevalence-age`

Blocks executable files that are not yet prevalent, old enough or on a trusted list, judged by cloud-delivered protection. Brand-new malware is caught this way, but so is any legitimate program that few people have run yet. Cloud protection must be on. Use Audit or Warn and review the audit view before considering Block.

- **Gamer impact (high):** High. Freshly patched games, indie and beta builds, mod managers and community tools can be blocked until their reputation builds up.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion>

### Use advanced protection against ransomware

`c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35` | key `ransomware`

Uses client and cloud heuristics to decide whether a file resembles ransomware. Signed files, files the cloud knows to be clean and prevalent files are not blocked, but unknown files without a positive reputation can be. Such blocks usually clear as reputation grows. Cloud protection must be on.

- **Gamer impact (medium):** Medium. Unsigned, little-known executables such as new indie games, mods or trainers can be blocked until they gain reputation. Audit first.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware>

### Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands

`d1e49aac-8f56-4280-b9ba-993a6d77406c` | key `psexec-wmi`

PsExec and WMI can start programs remotely, and malware uses them for command and control or to spread across a network. This rule blocks every process created that way. Some legitimate software, including updaters, hardware utilities and management scripts, also starts processes through WMI, so test it in Audit first.

- **Gamer impact (medium):** Medium. Launchers, updaters or hardware utilities that start helpers through WMI can break. Check the audit view before using Block.
- **Notes:** Never enable on PCs managed by Configuration Manager. Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands>

### Block all Office applications from creating child processes

`d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a` | key `office-child-processes`

Malicious documents usually run macros or exploit code that starts PowerShell, cmd or a downloaded payload. This rule blocks Office apps from creating child processes. Some add-ins and business macros do this legitimately, so audit first. It is only enforced when Office is installed under Program Files.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Office add-ins or macros that start Command Prompt, PowerShell or helper apps are blocked.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes>

### Block Office applications from creating executable content

`3b576869-a4ec-4529-8536-b80a7769e899` | key `office-executable-content`

Prevents Word, Excel and PowerPoint from saving malicious components to disk where they survive a restart, and blocks running untrusted files that macros wrote. It does not depend on where Office is installed. Audit first if you rely on macros that generate files.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Only Office documents and macros that save and run executable files are affected.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-office-applications-from-creating-executable-content>

### Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes

`75668c1f-73b5-4cf0-bb93-3ecf5cb7cc84` | key `office-injection`

Attackers inject code from Office into other processes so it runs disguised as a clean program. Microsoft knows of no legitimate business purpose for this. The rule applies to Word, Excel, OneNote and PowerPoint installed under Program Files, needs an Office restart to take effect and does not support Warn mode.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. A few security products (BeyondTrust Privilege Guard, Heimdal) are listed by Microsoft as incompatible.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes>

### Block Office communication application from creating child processes

`26190899-1602-49e8-8b27-eb1d0a1ce869` | key `outlook-child-processes`

Prevents Outlook from creating child processes, which blocks social-engineering payloads and the Outlook rules and forms exploits attackers use with stolen credentials. Normal mail features keep working. It is only enforced when Office is installed under Program Files.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Outlook add-ins that start external programs are blocked.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes>

### Block Win32 API calls from Office macros

`92e97fa1-2edf-4476-bdd6-9dd0b4dddc7b` | key `office-macro-win32`

Office VBA can call Win32 APIs, which malware abuses to launch shellcode without writing files. The rule blocks those calls from macros. Most people who use macros at all never need Win32 API calls, but audit first if you run complex business macros.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Only Office macros that call Windows APIs are affected.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-win32-api-calls-from-office-macros>

### Block Adobe Reader from creating child processes

`7674ba52-37eb-4a4f-a9a1-f0f9a1619a2c` | key `adobe-child-processes`

Malicious PDFs use social engineering or exploits to make Adobe Reader download and start a payload. Blocking Reader from creating child processes stops that path. Reader plug-ins or workflows that open other programs can be affected, so audit first if you depend on them.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None for games. Only Adobe Reader workflows that start other programs are affected.
- **Notes:** Limited exclusion support.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-adobe-reader-from-creating-child-processes>

### Block Webshell creation for Servers

`a8f5898e-1dc8-49a9-9878-85004b8a61e6` | key `webshell-servers`

Blocks web shell scripts on Windows servers that run Microsoft Exchange. It does not apply to Windows 11 clients, and Microsoft advises leaving it Not configured outside Defender for Endpoint management to avoid conflicts. iG Windows Tuner shows it for completeness and does not change it.

- **Gamer impact (none):** None. The rule only applies to Exchange servers.
- **Source:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-webshell-creation-for-servers>

## Exclusions

- **Per-rule exclusions** (recommended) are written to the documented Group Policy registry settings: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Windows Defender Exploit Guard\ASR\ASROnlyPerRuleExclusions` (value name = rule GUID, data = paths separated by `>`) plus the policy switch `ExploitGuard_ASR_ASROnlyPerRuleExclusions = 1`. When iG Windows Tuner runs as administrator it confirms through `Get-MpPreference` that Defender picked them up.
- **Global ASR exclusions** use `Add-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions` and apply to every rule.
- Refused: drive roots, the Windows folder, the whole Program Files folders, folders or wildcards inside user profiles and ProgramData, Downloads, Desktop, browser cache and temp folders, user environment variables, relative segments, quotes and the `>` separator. Folder exclusions must be at least two levels deep. Exclude the program file itself whenever possible.
- Defender applies exclusions when a program starts; restart the program after adding one. Antivirus scan exclusions are never added.

## Audit view

`-AsrAudit [-Days N]` and the GUI read the Defender Operational log (read-only): ASR 1121 (block), 1122 (audit), 1129 (Warn bypass); controlled folder access 1123/1127 (block), 1124/1128 (audit); network protection 1125 (audit), 1126 (block); 5007 (configuration change). Events are grouped by rule and program, with a next step: promote a quiet Audit rule (after at least 7 days of log coverage), add a per-rule exclusion for a trusted program's exact file, or ignore expected LSASS noise from Windows components.

## Security score

`-SecurityScore`, `-Report` and the dashboard. Pass earns the weight, Warn half, Fail nothing; not applicable, managed and unreadable checks are left out. Grades: Strong 90+, Good 75+, Fair 50+, Weak below.

| Check | Weight | Fix | Hint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Defender real-time protection | 15 | Virus & threat protection | Defender Antivirus is active with real-time protection on. |
| Tamper Protection | 8 | Virus & threat protection settings | Stops malware and tools from switching Defender protection off. Turn it on in Windows Security; iG Windows Tuner only reads it. |
| Security intelligence up to date | 4 | Protection updates | Defender definitions are at most 3 days old. |
| Cloud protection and PUA blocking | 5 | `sec.defender-hardening` | Cloud-delivered protection, safe sample submission and potentially unwanted app blocking are on. |
| Network protection | 4 | `sec.network-protection` | Blocks connections to known malicious domains from every app. |
| ASR standard protection rules in Block | 8 | ASR Center | The three ASR rules Microsoft recommends enabling in Block without testing are active. |
| ASR rules at their recommended mode | 4 | ASR Center | Every ASR rule is at least at the mode iG Windows Tuner recommends for a gaming PC (Block or Audit). |
| Windows Firewall on | 10 | `sec.firewall-on` | All firewall profiles are on and block unsolicited inbound traffic. |
| User Account Control | 10 | `sec.uac-on` | UAC is on and prompts on the secure desktop before programs get administrator rights. |
| Secure Boot | 8 | Enable Secure Boot in the BIOS/UEFI setup | Secure Boot is on, which blocks boot-level malware and is required by several kernel anti-cheats. |
| TPM 2.0 | 4 | Enable Intel PTT / AMD fTPM in the BIOS/UEFI setup | A ready TPM 2.0 protects keys for BitLocker and Windows Hello and is required by several anti-cheats. |
| Memory integrity (VBS/HVCI) | 8 | `sec.hvci-on` | Virtualization-based security and memory integrity are running and keep unsigned code out of the kernel. |
| LSA protection | 5 | `sec.lsa-protection` | LSASS runs as a protected process, so credential dumpers cannot read it. |
| Vulnerable driver blocklist | 4 | `sec.vulnerable-driver-blocklist` | Windows refuses to load drivers on Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist. |
| SmartScreen | 4 | `sec.smartscreen-on` | SmartScreen warns before unknown or malicious downloads and apps run. |
| Exploit protection system defaults | 4 | `sec.exploit-protection-defaults` | DEP, SEHOP, CFG and ASLR are at their Windows defaults (on). |
| WDigest credential caching off | 3 | `sec.wdigest-off` | Windows does not keep sign-in passwords in clear text for the legacy WDigest protocol. |
| SMB signing required, SMBv1 off | 3 | `sec.smb-hardening` | File sharing traffic is signed and the obsolete SMBv1 protocol is not installed. |
| Remote Desktop and Remote Assistance off | 2 | `sec.remote-access-off` | No incoming Remote Desktop or Remote Assistance connections are accepted. |
| LLMNR off | 2 | `sec.llmnr-off` | Windows does not answer link-local multicast name queries that attackers spoof to capture hashes. |
| AutoRun off | 2 | `sec.autorun-off` | USB drives and discs cannot start programs automatically. |
| BitLocker on the system drive | 4 | Settings > Privacy & security > Device encryption / BitLocker | The system drive is encrypted, so a stolen PC or drive does not expose your data. Back up the recovery key first. |
| Guest and built-in Administrator disabled | 3 | Computer Management > Local Users and Groups | The Guest account and the built-in Administrator (which runs without UAC prompts) are disabled. |
| Smart App Control | info | App & browser control > Smart App Control | Shown for information: blocks untrusted apps. It can only be turned on again with a clean install, so it is not scored. |
| Credential Guard | info | - | Shown for information: isolates credentials with VBS. Available on Enterprise and Education, not Windows 11 Pro. |

```

`docs/CHANGELOG.md`:

```md
# Changelog

## 2.0.0 (in progress)

### Renamed to iG Windows Tuner

- The project, GUI, reports and documentation are now called **iG Windows Tuner** (formerly AegisTune). Entry points: `iGWindowsTuner.ps1`, `Start-iGWindowsTuner.cmd`, module `src\iGWindowsTuner.psd1`; exported commands use the `Igwt` noun prefix (for example `Get-IgwtCatalog`, `Invoke-IgwtApply`); environment variables use `IGWT_`; the item `source` and overlay `basis` value `aegis` is now `igwt`.
- Data root `%ProgramData%\iGWindowsTuner` (logs fall back to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\iGWindowsTuner`). Backups in the old `%ProgramData%\AegisTune\Backups` stay listed and revertable, and a pending restart recorded there is still shown; nothing is written to the old folder.
- Snapshots record `tool: "iG Windows Tuner"`; snapshots that say `AegisTune` are still accepted. Objects the tool creates are named `iGWindowsTuner-...` (QoS policies, owned firewall rules); QoS policies created as `AegisTune-<game>` are detected, updated and removed under their old name.

### Management and diagnostic modules

- Services: every service with description, status, startup type, dependencies, a rating (Protected, Catalogued, Windows, installed by an app) and the catalog items and presets that touch it; startup type changes with a snapshot. Protected list in `data\manage\services.json`.
- Scheduled tasks: browse all tasks, disable or enable (never create or delete); security, update and anti-cheat tasks are refused. New catalog item `privacy.telemetry-tasks-off` (Advanced, Tier B).
- Persistence Inspector (read-only, Autoruns-style): Run/RunOnce (including WOW6432Node), Startup folders, non-Microsoft services, drivers and tasks, WMI event subscriptions, Winlogon Shell/Userinit, IFEO Debugger, AppInit_DLLs and browser extensions, with Authenticode status and severity. Startup entries, services and tasks can be disabled through their documented mechanisms; HTML/JSON export.
- Apps: installed Win32 and Appx apps; inbox app removal per user or provisioned with a snapshot and reversibility note; protected Store, App Installer, Xbox identity, Gaming Services, Windows Security, WebView2, frameworks and shell. Features and capabilities manager with a protected list.
- Windows Update: read-only status (services, pending restart, policies, history and failures) and new catalog item `privacy.defer-feature-90` (feature updates only).
- Network toolkit: adapter inspector with a description for every advanced property, user-initiated DNS benchmark and latency/jitter/loss test, firewall rule browser (app rules can be enabled or disabled; Windows rules never), read-only hosts-file viewer that flags unexpected entries.
- Diagnostics: DPC and ISR percentages from raw performance counters with top processes, reliability history, crashes (BugCheck, Kernel-Power 41, unexpected shutdowns, app crashes, minidump list), boot performance (event 100), driver inventory with date and signer. Full system report export (HTML and JSON).
- All changes go through `Invoke-IgwtManagedChange` (snapshot operation `Manage`, revert through `Invoke-IgwtRevert`, targets validated again on revert). 84 tweaks in total.
- CLI: `-Inventory Services|Tasks|Apps|Features|Firewall|Hosts|Adapters [-Search]`, `-Change <kind> -Target -Value [-Provisioned] [-DryRun]`, `-Persistence [-IncludeMicrosoft] [-ReportPath]`, `-Updates`, `-Diagnostics <areas> [-Days]`, `-SystemReport -ReportPath [-Quick]`, `-DnsBenchmark`, `-Latency <targets>`. GUI: Manage page (services, tasks, apps, persistence, firewall and hosts) and Diagnostics & Network page (overview, drivers, Windows Update, network tools, system report).
- Tests: `tests\Manage.Tests.ps1` (protection data, managed change round trips and refusals, tampered snapshot, inventories, persistence, update status, network toolkit, diagnostics, system report, catalog items, CLI argument checks).

### Expert controls and inspectors

- Read-only expert inspectors (`docs\INSPECTORS.md`): power plan (every processor setting of the active plan, hidden ones included, with Windows defaults, hidden flag and hardware blocks), interrupts (supported and current interrupt mode, MSI configuration, affinity policy and target CPUs), network queues (RSS, queues, buffers, discarded packets), kernel and memory (registry values with meaning, default and the catalog or rejected entry), timer, and crash dumps and page file.
- Power plan editor (Expert): 16 processor settings, values checked against the range `powercfg` reports, hardware overlays enforced, snapshot first (operation `Power`) and full revert; "Windows default" button and `-PowerDefault`.
- New System category: page file managed by Windows, small memory dumps, verbose status messages, stop code parameters on the blue screen. New items `power.show-processor-settings` and `gfx.gpu-msi` (Expert). 82 tweaks in total.
- Eleven new rejected entries from spec section 6 (hypervisor launch type off, processor idle disable, manual interrupt pinning, test signing and kernel debugging, IFEO edits, registry cleaners, hosts-file telemetry blocking, Prefetch cleaning, manual WinSxS/Installer deletion, disabling IPv6).
- CLI: `-Inspect All|Power|Interrupts|Network|Kernel|Timer|Crash [-Json]`, `-PowerSetting <alias> -Ac/-Dc/-PowerDefault [-AcknowledgeRisk] [-DryRun]`. GUI: Expert Inspectors page (tabs, power editor) and a System & Diagnostics category page.
- Tests: `tests\Inspectors.Tests.ps1` (parser including localized labels and UNKNOWN values, editor validation, overlay blocks, snapshot and revert, defaults resolution, interrupt, NIC, kernel, timer and crash inspectors with mocks) and new static checks (inspectors read-only, idle disable never editable).

### ASR Center and security modules

- ASR Center for all 19 Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction rules (`data\asr\rules.json`, `docs\ASR_CENTER.md`): current mode and where it comes from (local, Group Policy, MDM), recommendation, gamer-impact note, Warn and cloud limitations, and exclusions.
- Changes with a snapshot first and full revert: rule modes (Not configured, Audit, Warn where supported, Block; never an explicit Off), "apply recommendations" (never lowers a rule), per-rule exclusions (documented Group Policy registry settings, confirmed through Defender when elevated) and global ASR-only exclusions. Exclusions are validated: no drive roots, Windows folder, whole Program Files, user-writable folders or user variables.
- Read-only audit view: ASR, controlled folder access and network protection events from the Defender log, grouped by rule and program, with next steps (promote a quiet Audit rule, exclude a trusted program's exact file, ignore expected LSASS noise).
- Read-only security score (25 weighted checks, each with its fix: a catalog item, the ASR Center, Windows Security, firmware or Settings), local accounts audit and listening-ports report.
- Eight security items: exploit protection system defaults (repair-only), WDigest caching off, no anonymous enumeration, NTLMv2 only, Windows Script Host off, outbound firewall blocks for mshta/wscript/cscript/regsvr32/certutil, Print Spooler without inbound clients, Print Spooler off.
- `exploitSystem` and `processMitigation` accept `equivalentOn: ["NOTSET"]` for repair-only items.
- CLI: `-Asr` (with `-AsrRule`, `-AsrMode`, `-AsrRecommended`, `-AsrExclude`, `-AsrUnexclude`, `-DryRun`), `-AsrAudit [-Days]`, `-SecurityScore`, `-NetworkSurface`; the security score is part of `-Report` (console and HTML).
- GUI: ASR Center page (rule list, details, mode selector, exclusions, audit view with "use as exclusion") and a Security score card on the dashboard.
- Tests: `tests\Asr.Tests.ps1` (catalog, status, path validation, changes and reverts with stateful Defender mocks in TestRegistry, audit grouping, score, accounts, network surface) and new static checks (no duplicate function names, no `$name?` in strings, ASR code read-only where it should be).

### Action handlers

- 14 new action types, each with detect, snapshot, apply and restore: `storageSense`, `wufbPolicy`, `deviceInterrupt`, `serviceSet` (registry/service composites), `powercfgAttribute`, `powercfgSettingAcDc`, `scheduledTask`, `firewallRule`, `appx`, `winget`, `capability`, `processMitigation`, `exploitSystem`, `cleanerRule`; plus a read-only `DefaultApp` check.
- Safety limits in code and validation: protected services, tasks and apps; firewall Block rules and group disabling only; system exploit protection only ON; device interrupts only on GPU/NIC/USB controllers that declare MSI support, never the boot controller; winget only through fixed arguments; no BCD writes.
- The Storage Sense tweaks use the typed `storageSense` action. `docs\TWEAKS.md` describes every new action type.
- Tests: `tests\Handlers.Tests.ps1` round-trips every handler (detect, snapshot through JSON, apply, detect, restore, detect) in TestRegistry or with stateful mocks, and checks the validation rules.

### Hardware profile engine

- Read-only hardware facts (CPU, active GPUs, network controllers, memory, battery/chassis, Modern Standby, system disk, VM) turned into hardware tags by data-driven rules (`data\hardware\detection.json`). This PC: `intel.hybrid`, `intel.raptorlake.desktop`, `gpu.nvidia`, `nic.marvell`, `storage.nvme`, `ram.32`, `formfactor.desktop`.
- 15 hardware overlays with sources (`data\hardware\overlays.json`, `docs\HARDWARE.md`): Intel hybrid scheduling, Raptor Lake Vmin Shift protection, AMD X3D dual-CCD core steering, AMD chipset driver, Modern Standby and laptop power, SysMain on slow disks or low RAM, virtual machines, Intel Arc Resizable BAR, NVIDIA Reflex, AMD Anti-Lag 2, Intel I225/I226, Killer, Realtek/Marvell drivers.
- Presets resolve as intent preset -> hardware overlays -> your add-ons. Blocked items are Not applicable (already-applied ones can still be turned off); overlay adds respect the preset's level ceiling, anti-cheat policy and exclusions.
- `-Hardware` (read-only profile, `-Json` facts), hardware section in `-Report` (console and HTML), overlay reasons and guidance in `-Preset ... -DryRun`, and a Hardware profile card on the GUI dashboard. Preset cards and staging use the resolved selection.
- Tests: `tests\Hardware.Tests.ps1` with six fixtures (this PC, AMD X3D dual-CCD desktop, Intel laptop, AMD laptop, Intel Arc desktop, VM).

### Schema v2 and migration

- All data files are schema v2 (`docs\SCHEMA.md`): `level` (Standard/Advanced/Expert/Lab), `antiCheat` ("safe", "unknown" or the anti-cheats it breaks), `reversible`, `sideEffects`, `source` (+ attribution), `hardware` tags and `appliesTo.conditions`. Presets are intent presets (`include`, `exclude`, `levelCeiling`, `antiCheatPolicy`). New hardware tag vocabulary in `data\hardware\tags.json`.
- Automatic migration: v1 catalog files, presets, cleaner rules and snapshots are upgraded in memory when read. `tools\Convert-IgwtV1Data.ps1` rewrites v1 data files (idempotent) and writes schema 2 copies of snapshots to another folder; originals are never changed.
- Snapshots are schema 2 (catalog schema, hardware tags, item level per entry). 1.0 snapshots still revert exactly; a real 1.0 snapshot is a test fixture.
- Validation: every tweak, cleaner rule, preset and hardware tag needs a hint (140 characters or fewer) and a description; valid level, tier, anti-cheat field, reversibility, source and known hardware tags; anti-cheat-breaking items must be Lab; no Lab, rejected or non-safe items in gaming presets.
- GUI shows level badges and the specific anti-cheat impact; every button and input has a tooltip. `-ListTweaks` shows Level, AntiCheat and Reversible, and dry-run plans include Level.

### Cleaning engine

- New allow-list cleaner with 44 rules in six categories (System, Gaming, Browsers, Apps, Developer, Downloads), each with a hint, description and side effects (`docs\CLEANER.md`).
- Two-phase operation: `Invoke-IgwtCleanerScan` sizes everything and deletes nothing; `Invoke-IgwtCleanerClean` deletes only the scanned files after re-validating each one. Deleted paths are logged to `Logs\Cleaner-<time>.jsonl` (10 logs kept, older ones zipped).
- Safety core: path canonicalization (including 8.3 names), hard denylist, no reparse-point following, cloud-placeholder skip, unchanged-since-scan check, no recursive deletes, never closes apps, services always restarted.
- Special methods through supported tools: Recycle Bin, Delivery Optimization cache, DISM component cleanup (with an Expert ResetBase rule), old driver packages (pnputil without /force), and size-only guidance for Windows.old and Docker.
- Read-only disk analyzer (`Get-IgwtDiskUsage`): largest folders and files, junction-safe.
- Storage Sense category with three documented policy tweaks (weekly temp cleanup, Recycle Bin after 30 days, expert Downloads threshold).
- CLI: `-Clean` (`-Scan`/`-DryRun` read-only, `-CleanRule`, `-CleanLevel`, `-IncludeOptIn`, `-AllUsers`, `-Yes`) and `-Analyze <path> -Top N`.
- GUI: Cleaner, Storage Sense and Disk Analyzer pages with cancel support.
- Tests: `tests\Cleaner.Tests.ps1` (fixtures in TestDrive only; traversal, injection, junction swap, locked, offline and changed files, service restore, special methods, analyzer, Storage Sense apply/revert in TestRegistry) plus new static safety checks.

## 1.0.0 (2026-10-16)

First release.

- Data-driven engine with 15 action types: registry, registryListMerge, adapterRegistry, netAdapterPower, powercfgScheme, powercfgSetting, service, netAdapterAdvanced, netQosPolicy, dnsDoh, mpPreference, asrRule, optionalFeature, custom and check.
- 65 catalog tweaks (43 Tier A, 22 Tier B) in 6 categories; 3 presets (Competitive, Balanced, Hardened); 28 documented rejected tweaks.
- Snapshot of exact previous values (type, data, absent, created keys) before every change, plus a System Restore point; atomic per-tweak rollback; idempotent apply; revert by id, last apply or snapshot file; reset to documented Windows defaults.
- Read-only health report (console, HTML, JSON): OS, CPU microcode (Vmin Shift 0x12F check), memory, BIOS, TPM, Secure Boot and the 2023 certificate status, VBS/HVCI/IOMMU, GPU/ReBAR/HAGS/refresh rate, NIC/link speed/EEE, storage/TRIM/free space, Defender/firewall/UAC/LSA/BitLocker, and an anti-cheat readiness matrix.
- WPF GUI with background worker, staged changes, preview, search and filters, Startup Apps, Backups & Logs, and the Rejected Tweaks explainer.
- Pester 5 suite (TestRegistry plus mocks), PSScriptAnalyzer settings, Windows Sandbox end-to-end test, optional Authenticode signing with SHA256 manifest, and generated catalog docs.

`docs/CLEANER.md`:

```md
# iG Windows Tuner cleaner rules

> Generated by `tools\Build-Docs.ps1` from `data\cleaner\*.json`. Do not edit by hand.

44 allow-list rules. Every rule names the folders it may clean; nothing outside them is ever touched. The cleaner always scans first (read-only) and then deletes only the files that scan found, re-checking each file right before it is deleted.

## Safety model

- Allow-list only: a file is deleted only if its canonical path lies strictly inside one of the rule's roots, and the roots are resolved again at clean time.
- Paths are canonicalized (`..`, 8.3 short names) before any check; relative, UNC and device paths are refused.
- A hard denylist in the deletion primitive protects drive roots, Windows (except Temp, the update download cache, CBS/DISM logs and crash dumps), Program Files (except the Steam shader cache, logs and dumps), ProgramData roots, Defender folders, profile roots, Documents, Desktop, Pictures, Music, Videos, Saved Games, OneDrive and the Downloads folder (opt-in rule only).
- Browser profiles: only cache folders (Cache, Code Cache, GPU and shader caches, cache2) are cleaned. Cookies, history, passwords and extensions are never touched.
- Junctions, symbolic links and mount points are never followed or deleted; each file's parent chain is re-checked for reparse points right before deletion.
- Cloud placeholders and offline files are skipped, so cleaning never triggers a download.
- Files that changed since the scan, are younger than the rule's minimum age, are in use, or are read-only are skipped.
- Only single files and empty folders are deleted; there is no recursive delete. Apps are never closed (rules that need an app closed are skipped while it runs). Services are stopped only for rules that declare them and are always restarted.
- Every deleted path is written to `Logs\Cleaner-<time>.jsonl`.

| Category | Rules | On by default |
|---|---|---|
| System | 14 | 5 |
| Gaming | 12 | 2 |
| Browsers | 6 | 0 |
| Apps | 3 | 0 |
| Developer | 8 | 0 |
| Downloads | 1 | 0 |

## System

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| `clean.component-store` | Component store cleanup (DISM) | Advanced | no | dism | yes | - |
| `clean.component-store-resetbase` | Component store cleanup with /ResetBase | Expert | no | dism | yes | - |
| `clean.delivery-optimization` | Delivery Optimization cache | Standard | yes | deliveryOptimization | yes | - |
| `clean.driver-store` | Old driver packages | Expert | no | driverStore | yes | - |
| `clean.memory-dumps` | Crash dumps (minidumps and live kernel reports) | Advanced | no | files | yes | - |
